name: Amazon DynamoDB
model: Tables of items (JSON-like attribute maps, max 400 KB) found by partition key plus optional sort key; no joins, no SQL
engine_note: Each partition is a Multi-Paxos replication group of 3 replicas; each replica holds a write-ahead log and a B-tree of the key-value data
consistency: Single-item writes are durable on return (quorum of logs). Reads are eventually consistent by default; strongly consistent reads are an option (not on GSIs). Transactions: up to 100 items, serializable, one Region. Global tables are async by default.
scaling: Serverless: tables split into partitions by key automatically, on-demand or provisioned capacity; global tables replicate across Regions.
version_note: 2026-10-01: export to S3 supports filtered exports. Multi-Region strong consistency for global tables went GA 2025-06-30 (preview 2024-12-03).
reach: Reach for it when you are on AWS and know your access patterns up front: lookups by key at any scale with no servers or vacuum to manage.
avoid: Avoid when you need ad hoc queries, joins or analytics, or your access patterns are still changing; each new pattern needs an index or a redesign.
escape: You want key lookups at any scale with zero servers to run, and you can live without joins.
chat: Messages keyed by chat id and sorted by timestamp, plus per-user usage counters, if the app is all-in on AWS.
notes: Engine detail from the USENIX ATC 2022 paper (Elhemali et al.): 'storage replicas that contain both the write-ahead logs and the B-tree'; AWS may have changed internals since. Transactions are serializable against single-item ops but read committed against Query/Scan/BatchGet. In global tables (default MREC mode) transactions are atomic only in the Region that ran them and conflicts are last writer wins; MRSC tables do not support transactions. No Jepsen report. The 2007 Dynamo paper describes a different, older system; do not confuse it with DynamoDB.
